title: Type-A Hecke Specht Modules and Cellular Bases

items.title: Cellular bases and cell modules
items.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and $A$ a unital $R$-algebra ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) which is free as an $R$-module on a finite set $C=\{c^{\lambda}_{st}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ s,t\in T(\lambda)\}$, where $(\Lambda,\unrhd)$ is a finite poset ([[def-partial-order]]; its strict order is written $\rhd$) and each $T(\lambda)$ is a finite set. For $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ be the $R$-submodule of $A$ spanned by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with $\mu\rhd\lambda$. Then $(C,\Lambda)$ is a **cellular basis** of $A$, and $A$ is a **cellular algebra**, if: (i) the $R$-linear map $i:A\to A$ with $i(c^{\lambda}_{st})=c^{\lambda}_{ts}$ for all $\lambda,s,t$ is an algebra anti-automorphism of $A$, i.e. $i(ab)=i(b)i(a)$ and $i(1)=1$ (equivalently $i$ is an isomorphism of $A$ with the opposite algebra; the displayed formula forces $i^2=\mathrm{id}$); and (ii) for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$, every $t\in T(\lambda)$ and every $a\in A$ there exist $r_v\in R$ ($v\in T(\lambda)$) with $$c^{\lambda}_{st}\,a\equiv\sum_{v\in T(\lambda)}r_v\,c^{\lambda}_{sv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}.$$

**Cell modules.** For $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $C^{\lambda}$ be the free $R$-module with basis $\{c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_{tt}:t\in T(\lambda)\}$; condition (ii) makes $C^{\lambda}$ a right $A$-module by $c^{\lambda}_t a:=\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_v$ when $c^{\lambda}_{tt}a\equiv\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_{tv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$, and it makes $C^{\lambda}$ a left $A$-module via $i$. The module $C^{\lambda}$ is the **(right) cell module** of $\lambda$, and $A^{\unrhd\lambda}/A^{\rhd\lambda}\cong C^{\lambda}\otimes_R C^{\lambda}$ via $c^{\lambda}_{st}+A^{\rhd\lambda}\mapsto c^{\lambda}_s\otimes c^{\lambda}_t$. A cellular algebra may have several cellular bases.
items.strategy: A definition item recording the Graham-Lehrer axioms exactly as used later. The only point needing care is that the displayed formula really defines a module action: this is Corollary 2.3(i) of the source, obtained by applying the anti-automorphism (i) to the triangular relation; the ideal identification is the display after (2.5). In every application on this page $A=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ is a free $R$-module of finite rank. No choice is used.

Mathas-Soriano, Seminormal forms and Gram determinants for cellular algebras, sections 2.8-2.15 (the Graham-Lehrer axioms in the form used here), pp. 4-7

items.title: e-regular and e-restricted partitions
items.statement: Let $e\in\{2,3,4,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition with parts $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots$ and conjugate $\lambda'$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Then $\lambda$ is **$e$-regular** when every positive integer occurs as a part of $\lambda$ fewer than $e$ times, i.e. $z_j(\lambda)<e$ for every $j\ge1$, and **$e$-restricted** when $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<e$ for every $i\ge1$ (with $\lambda_i:=0$ for $i>\ell(\lambda)$). For finite $e$ these are exactly the $p$-regular and $p$-restricted notions of [[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]] with $p=e$, and $\lambda$ is $e$-restricted if and only if its conjugate $\lambda'$ is $e$-regular. For $e=\infty$ both conditions are vacuous, so every partition is both $e$-regular and $e$-restricted.
items.strategy: A definition item specialising the published $p$-regular/$p$-restricted definitions along the prime $p=e$; the conjugate equivalence is the finite-$e$ case of the corresponding statement for partitions ([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]]). No choice is used.

references.title: Mathas, Iwahori-Hecke Algebras and Schur Algebras of the Symmetric Group, the definition of $e$-restricted partitions in Chapter 3 section 4, printed p. 32
Kleshchev, Symmetric groups and related Hecke algebras, section 5.3 (e-restricted labels and Remark 5.5), p. 24

items.title: The quantum characteristic of an invertible Hecke parameter
items.statement:
Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{	imes}$ an invertible element. The **quantum characteristic** $e=e(F,q)$ is the least integer $e\ge2$ such that $1+q+\cdots+q^{e-1}=0$ in $F$, and $e:=\infty$ when no such integer exists ([[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]], [[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Since $[1]_q=1
e0$, the least positive integer $e$ with $[e]_q=0$, when it exists, automatically satisfies $e\ge2$, so the two formulations coincide. Concretely: (i) if $q
e1$ then $[m]_q=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ for all $m\ge0$, so a finite $e$ exists exactly when $q$ is a root of unity and then $e$ is the multiplicative order of $q$ in $F^{	imes}$; (ii) if $q=1$ then $[m]_1=m$, so $e=\operatorname{char}(F)$ when $\operatorname{char}(F)>0$ and $e=\infty$ when $\operatorname{char}(F)=0$ ([[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]]). If $e<\infty$ then $q
e1$ implies $q^e=1$, and hence $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ for every integer $m$; in particular the quantum characteristic, not merely the multiplicative order, is the parameter governing the modular representation theory of the Hecke algebra. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: A definition item; the identities $[m]_q=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ for $q\ne1$ and $[m]_1=m$ are the definition of the quantum integers, and the displayed equivalences are immediate case checks. The last sentence records the reduction $[m+e]_q=[m]_q+q^m[e]_q$ that every later residue computation uses. No choice is used.

references.title: Mathas, Iwahori-Hecke Algebras and Schur Algebras of the Symmetric Group, (3.28) with the surrounding quantum-integer conventions, printed pp. 27 and 56
Kleshchev, Symmetric groups and related Hecke algebras, section 5.3: the quantum characteristic e, p. 24

items.title: Decompositions of the identity into primitive central idempotents are unique
items.statement: Let $A$ be a unital ring, with centre $Z(A):=\{z\in A: za=az	ext{ for all }a\in A\}$. Suppose that $$1=e_1+\cdots+e_k=f_1+\cdots+f_\ell$$ where $\{e_1,\dots,e_k\}$ and $\{f_1,\dots,f_\ell\}$ are finite families of pairwise orthogonal central idempotents of $A$ that are primitive among central idempotents: each is nonzero and admits no decomposition as a sum of two nonzero orthogonal central idempotents (zero parts are omitted). Then $k=\ell$ and there is a bijection $\sigma$ of the index sets with $e_i=f_{\sigma(i)}$ for all $i$; in particular the decomposition of $1$ into primitive central idempotents is unique up to order. No choice principle is used, the families being finite.
items.strategy: For each pair, $e_if_j$ is an idempotent (all factors commute) and $\sum_j e_if_j=e_i$ with pairwise orthogonal terms; primitivity of $e_i$ forces all but one term to vanish, say $e_i=e_if_{j(i)}$. Symmetrically each $f_j$ admits exactly one $i$ with $f_j=f_je_i$. The map $i\mapsto j(i)$ is injective (otherwise some $f_j$ would split as a sum of two nonzero orthogonal idempotents), and counting the two decompositions of $1$ shows that it is a bijection; then $e_i=e_if_{j(i)}=f_{j(i)}e_i=f_{j(i)}$ because all idempotents involved are central, so the families coincide. No choice is used.

references.title: Andrew Mathas, Iwahori-Hecke Algebras and Schur Algebras of the Symmetric Group, Chapter 5 section 3 (block conventions) and the standard uniqueness of primitive central orthogonal decompositions, printed pp. 53-54
Jacobsen, Block fusion systems and the center of the group ring, sections 1.1 and 2.2 (primitive idempotent decompositions), pp. 3-8 and 13-18

items.title: The identity of a finite-dimensional algebra decomposes into primitive central idempotents
items.statement: Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital $F$-algebra with centre $Z(A):=\{z\in A:za=az	ext{ for all }a\in A\}$ ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). Then $Z(A)$ is a finite-dimensional commutative $F$-algebra, and the identity $1\in Z(A)$ admits a decomposition $$1=e_1+\cdots+e_k$$ into pairwise orthogonal primitive central idempotents of $A$: each $e_i$ is a nonzero idempotent of $Z(A)$ that is not the sum of two nonzero orthogonal idempotents of $Z(A)$. No semisimplicity of $A$ is assumed and no choice principle is used.
items.strategy: A subset of $Z(A)$ that is linearly independent over $F$ is linearly independent in the finite-dimensional space $A$, so it has at most $\dim_FA$ elements and $Z(A)$ is a finite-dimensional commutative $F$-algebra; its idempotents are exactly the central idempotents of $A$. Start with the family $\{1\}$ and split any non-primitive member $e$ as $e=u+v$ with $u,v$ nonzero orthogonal idempotents of $Z(A)$. The corners $uZ(A)u$ and $vZ(A)v$ are subspaces of $eZ(A)e$ of strictly smaller dimension (multiplication by $u$ kills $v$ but fixes $uZ(A)u$), and a mutually orthogonal family of nonzero idempotents is linearly independent, so the process terminates after at most $\dim_FZ(A)$ splits. The terminal family is the asserted decomposition and every member is primitive by construction. This is the standard finite-dimensional dimension-descent argument applied to the centre; the same argument for arbitrary finite-dimensional algebras is recorded in the published literature cited below. No choice is used.

references.title: Mathas, Iwahori-Hecke Algebras and Schur Algebras of the Symmetric Group, Chapter 5 section 3 (block conventions and primitive central idempotents), printed pp. 53-54
Jacobsen, Block fusion systems and the center of the group ring, sections 1.1 and 2.2 (finite-dimensional primitive idempotent decompositions), pp. 3-8 and 13-18

items.title: The star anti-automorphism of the type-A Hecke algebra
items.statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, and let $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ be the specialized type-A Hecke algebra with generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ and relations $T_i^2=(q-1)T_i+q$, the braid relations and the distant commutations ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Then the assignment $T_i\mapsto T_i$ ($1\le i<n$) extends uniquely to an $R$-algebra anti-automorphism $*:H\to H$, i.e. an $R$-linear map with $(ab)^*=b^*a^*$ and $1^*=1$; it is an involution, $**=\mathrm{id}_H$, and on the standard basis $$T_w^{*}=T_{w^{-1}}\qquad(w\in S_n).$$ In particular $(T_wT_{w^{-1}})^*=T_wT_{w^{-1}}$ and, for the symmetrizers $m_\lambda=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}T_w$, one has $m_\lambda^*=m_\lambda$.
items.strategy: The presentation ideal of $H$ is stable under reversal of products: the quadratic, braid and distant-commutation relators are palindromic, so the universal property of the presented algebra applied to $H^{\mathrm{op}}$ yields a unique algebra homomorphism $H\to H^{\mathrm{op}}$ sending each $T_i$ to $T_i$, i.e. an anti-automorphism $*$ of $H$. Since $*$ fixes a generating set, $**$ fixes a generating set and hence is the identity. For a reduced word $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_\ell}$ one has $T_w=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_\ell}$ by definition, so $T_w^*=T_{i_\ell}\cdots T_{i_1}=T_{w^{-1}}$, the reversed word being reduced for $w^{-1}$. This is Mathas, Chapter 3 section 2, where $*$ is the $R$-linear antiautomorphism determined by $T_i^*=T_i$ and $T_w^*=T_{w^{-1}}$; no choice is used.

references.title: Mathas, Iwahori-Hecke Algebras and Schur Algebras of the Symmetric Group, Chapter 3 section 2: the antiautomorphism with $T_i^*=T_i$, $T_w^*=T_{w^{-1}}$, printed pp. 20-25

items.title: Blocks of a finite-dimensional algebra via primitive central idempotents
items.statement: Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital $F$-algebra with centre $Z(A):=\{z\in A:za=az	ext{ for all }a\in A\}$ ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). A **central idempotent** of $A$ is an idempotent $e\in Z(A)$; it is **primitive** when $e\ne0$ and $e$ is not the sum of two nonzero orthogonal central idempotents. Then $Z(A)$ is a finite-dimensional commutative $F$-algebra, so $1\in Z(A)$ admits a decomposition $$1=e_1+\cdots+e_k$$ into pairwise orthogonal primitive central idempotents ([[lem-the-identity-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-decomposes-into-primitive-central-idempotents]]), and this decomposition is unique up to order ([[lem-central-idempotent-decompositions-of-one-are-unique]]). A **block** of $A$ is the two-sided ideal $B=eA=Ae$ cut out by a primitive central idempotent $e$. The blocks are pairwise orthogonal two-sided ideals, $A=B_1\oplus\cdots\oplus B_k$ as $F$-algebras with units $e_i$, each $B_i$ is an indecomposable two-sided ideal, and for every (not necessarily finite-dimensional) $A$-module $M$ one has $M=\bigoplus_{i=1}^ke_iM$ as $A$-modules; a simple $A$-module $S$ satisfies $e_iS\ne0$ for exactly one $i$ and then $S=e_iS$ lies in the corresponding block. Nothing here asserts that a block is semisimple or simple, and the construction is choice-free.
items.strategy: A definition item whose consistency is supplied by its dependencies: the preceding primitive-idempotent decomposition lemma applied to the commutative finite-dimensional $F$-algebra $Z(A)$ produces the primitive central idempotents (its primitive idempotents are exactly the primitive central idempotents of $A$), and the uniqueness lemma makes the block partition canonical. The module decomposition is idempotent calculus: $\sum_ie_i=1$ gives $M=\sum_ie_iM$, orthogonality gives directness, and a nonzero simple $S$ has $e_iS=S$ whenever $e_iS\ne0$. This avoids the Artinian structure theorem and hence uses no choice principle. The conventions follow Mathas, Chapter 5 section 3 (printed pp. 53-54).

references.title: Mathas, Iwahori-Hecke Algebras and Schur Algebras of the Symmetric Group, Chapter 5 section 3 (block conventions for $S(d,n)$ and $H$), printed pp. 53-54
Jacobsen, Block fusion systems and the center of the group ring, sections 1.1 and 2.2 (finite-dimensional primitive idempotent decompositions), pp. 3-8 and 13-18

items.title: Hecke Jucys-Murphy elements and q-contents
items.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). For $1\le k\le n$ define $$L_1:=0,\qquad L_k:=q^{-1}T_{(k-1,k)}+q^{-2}T_{(k-2,k)}+\cdots+q^{1-k}T_{(1,k)}\in H\quad(k\ge2),$$ where $T_{(i,k)}$ is the standard basis element indexed by the transposition $(i\ k)$ ([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). The $L_k$ are the **Hecke Jucys-Murphy elements**. They are fixed by the star anti-automorphism $T_w^*=T_{w^{-1}}$ ([[lem-the-star-antiautomorphism-of-the-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); they commute pairwise and every symmetric polynomial in $L_1,\dots,L_n$ with coefficients in $R$ is central in $H$ ([[thm-hecke-jucys-murphy-action-is-dominance-triangular]]).

**q-contents.** The quantum integers $[m]_q$ for $m\ge0$ are those of [[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]]; extend the definition to negative indices by $[-m]_q:=-q^{-m}[m]_q$ for $m>0$, so that $[m]_q=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ for all $m\in\mathbb Z$ when $q\ne1$, and $[m]_1=m$ for all $m\in\mathbb Z$. For a standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ and $1\le k\le n$ let $\operatorname{content}_t(k)=c-r$ be the content of the node carrying $k$ ([[def-content-vector-of-a-standard-tableau]]) and define the **q-content value** $[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q$. If $e=e(F,q)<\infty$ for a field $F$ then $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ for every $m\in\mathbb Z$, so the q-content value depends only on the residue of the content modulo $e$. At $q=1$ the specialization $T_w\mapsto w$ of [[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]] sends $L_k$ to the ordinary Jucys-Murphy element $X_k=\sum_{j<k}(j\ k)$ ([[def-jucys-murphy-elements-of-the-symmetric-group-algebra]]), and $[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_1=\operatorname{content}_t(k)$.
items.strategy: A definition item. Star-invariance is immediate from $T_{(i,k)}^*=T_{(i,k)}$ and the symmetry of the coefficients; commutation and centrality are deferred to [[thm-hecke-jucys-murphy-action-is-dominance-triangular]]; the $q=1$ limit is the substitution $q^{i-k}\mapsto1$ followed by $T_{(i,k)}\mapsto(i\ k)$. The negative-index extension is the standard convention of the source (3.27). No choice is used.

references.title: Mathas, Iwahori-Hecke Algebras and Schur Algebras of the Symmetric Group, the definition of $L_k$, (3.27)-(3.28) and Corollary 3.25, printed pp. 26-28
Mathas-Soriano, Seminormal forms and Gram determinants for cellular algebras, section 2.15 (the Hecke JM family and q-contents), pp. 6-7

items.title: Murphy elements and Murphy tableau elements
items.statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ with standard basis $\{T_w\}$ and star anti-automorphism $*$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], [[lem-the-star-antiautomorphism-of-the-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). For a composition (in particular a partition) $\mu$ of $n$ put $m_\mu:=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_w\in H$, the **row symmetrizer** of the standard Young subgroup $S_\mu$ ([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]); the sum has $|S_\mu|=\prod_i\mu_i!$ terms. For a row-standard $\mu$-tableau $s$ ([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]) let $d(s)\in S_n$ be the unique permutation of minimal length with $s=t^{\mu}d(s)$, where $t^{\mu}$ is the row-standard tableau obtained by entering $1,2,\dots,n$ in increasing order from left to right along the rows; $d(s)$ is the distinguished right-coset representative of $S_\mu$ in $S_n$ and $S_\mu$ is the stabiliser of $t^\mu$ ([[def-row-and-column-stabilizers-of-a-tableau]]). For row-standard $\mu$-tableaux $s,t$ define the **Murphy element** $$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^{*}\,m_{\mu}\,T_{d(t)}\in H,$$ and for a standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ shorten $m_t:=m_{tt}=T_{d(t)}^{*}m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$. Then $m_{st}^{*}=m_{ts}$ for all row-standard $s,t$ of the same shape, and $m_\mu T_w=q^{\ell(w)}m_\mu$ for every $w\in S_\mu$.
items.strategy: A definition item. The existence and uniqueness of $d(s)$, and the identity $\ell(wd)=\ell(w)+\ell(d)$ for $w\in S_\mu$, $d\in D_\mu$, are Proposition 3.3 and Corollary 3.4 of the source; $m_\mu T_w=q^{\ell(w)}m_\mu$ is Lemma 3.2, and the symmetry $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$ is immediate from $**=\mathrm{id}$. No choice is used.

references.title: Mathas, Iwahori-Hecke Algebras and Schur Algebras of the Symmetric Group, Chapter 3 sections 1-2: Lemma 3.2, Proposition 3.3, Corollary 3.4 and the definition of $m_{st}$, printed pp. 18-21

items.title: The cell form is associative and its radical is a submodule
items.statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $A$ a cellular $R$-algebra with cellular basis $(C,\Lambda)$ and cell modules $C^{\lambda}$ ([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For each $\lambda\in\Lambda$ there is a unique $R$-bilinear form $$\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda:C^{\lambda}\times C^{\lambda}\longrightarrow R$$ with $$c^{\lambda}_{us}c^{\lambda}_{tv}\equiv\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda\,c^{\lambda}_{uv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$$ for all $s,t,u,v\in T(\lambda)$; in particular the right hand side is independent of $u$ and $v$, and $\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda$ depends only on $s,t$. This form is (i) symmetric, $\langle x,y\rangle_\lambda=\langle y,x\rangle_\lambda$; (ii) associative, $\langle xa,y\rangle_\lambda=\langle x,\,i(a)y\rangle_\lambda$ for all $a\in A$ (and dually for the left action); (iii) characterised by $x\,c^{\lambda}_{uv}=\langle x,c^{\lambda}_u\rangle_\lambda\,c^{\lambda}_v$ for $x\in C^{\lambda}$; and (iv) its radical $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}:=\{x\in C^{\lambda}:\langle x,y\rangle_\lambda=0\text{ for all }y\in C^{\lambda}\}$ is an $A$-submodule of $C^{\lambda}$, namely the kernel of $x\mapsto\langle x,-\rangle_\lambda$.
items.strategy: Uniqueness and independence of $u,v$: multiply $c^{\lambda}_{us}c^{\lambda}_{tv}$ on the left by $c^{\lambda}_{wu}$ and compare the two resulting expressions inside the free quotient $A^{\unrhd\lambda}/A^{\rhd\lambda}$ using (2.1). Symmetry: apply the anti-automorphism $i$ to $c^{\lambda}_{us}c^{\lambda}_{tv}\equiv\langle c_s,c_t\rangle c_{uv}$ and use the stability of $A^{\rhd\lambda}$. Associativity is the comparison of the two ways to associate $c^{\lambda}_{us}(c^{\lambda}_{tv}a)$ modulo $A^{\rhd\lambda}$. For (iv), (iii) shows that for fixed $y$ the map $x\mapsto\langle x,y\rangle_\lambda$ is $A$-linear where defined, so its kernel is a submodule; the radical is the intersection of these kernels. This is Mathas, Corollary 2.3(iv), (2.6), Proposition 2.7 and Lemma 2.8, printed pp. 10-11; no choice is used.

references.title: Mathas, Iwahori-Hecke Algebras and Schur Algebras of the Symmetric Group, Corollary 2.3(iv), (2.6), Proposition 2.7, Lemma 2.8, printed pp. 10-11
Mathas-Soriano, Seminormal forms and Gram determinants for cellular algebras, sections 3.1-3.7 (cell forms and their radicals), pp. 9-11

items.title: The type-A q-Schur algebra and its Weyl modules
items.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{	imes}$, $d,n\ge0$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Let $\Lambda(d,n)$ be the set of compositions $\mu=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_d)$ of $n$ (so $\mu_i\in\mathbb N$ and $\sum_i\mu_i=n$). For $\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)$ let $m_\mu=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_w$ ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]) and let $M^{\mu}:=m_\mu H$ be the right ideal it generates, the **(Hecke) permutation module**; $M^{\mu}$ is free over $R$ with basis $\{m_\mu T_{d(t)}:t	ext{ row-standard }\mu	ext{-tableau}\}$ and is the Hecke analogue of the module induced from the trivial representation of the Young subgroup ([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]).

Here is the freeness statement in detail: the cosets $S_\mu d$ with $d\in D_\mu$ partition $S_n$, and $\ell(ud)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$ for $u\in S_\mu$, $d\in D_\mu$ ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]), so the standard basis theorem ([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]) gives $T_uT_{d(t)}=T_{ud(t)}$ and $m_\mu T_{d(t)}=\sum_{u\in S_\mu}T_{u\,d(t)}$; these are the standard basis elements indexed by the single coset $S_\mu d(t)$, and the cosets are disjoint, whence $M^\mu= igoplus_tR\,m_\mu T_{d(t)}$ is free with the displayed basis as $t$ runs over the row-standard $\mu$-tableaux.

items.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Let $\Lambda$ be the set of partitions
of $n$ ordered by dominance $\unrhd$
([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]), and for $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let
$T(\lambda)=\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$ be the set of standard $\lambda$-tableaux
([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). Then the **Murphy basis
theorem** holds: the family
$$\mathcal M=\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$$
is an $R$-basis of $H$, and $(\mathcal M,\Lambda)$ is a cellular basis of $H$ in
the sense of [[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]. Explicitly:
(i) $m_{st}^{*}=m_{ts}$ for all $\lambda$ and $s,t$; and (ii) for every
$\lambda$, every $t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$ and every $h\in H$ there exist
$r_v\in R$ with
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}},$$
where $H^{\rhd\lambda}$ is spanned by the $m_{uv}$ with $\mu\rhd\lambda$. The
theorem holds over every commutative coefficient ring with $q\in R^{\times}$
and assumes no semisimplicity; the total number of Murphy elements is
$\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}|\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)|^2=n!$
([[cor-sum-of-squares-of-standard-tableau-numbers]]), matching the rank of $H$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A commutative ring $R$, a unit $q$, the type-A Hecke algebra and the Murphy elements $m_{st}=T_{d(s)}^*x_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ in the Statement.

[F1] The independent integral construction proves that these exact elements form a base-change-compatible basis; their dominance spans are two-sided ideals, star interchanges the indices, and their multiplication satisfies the fixed-first-index cell law over every commutative coefficient ring with unit parameter ([[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]]).

[F2] The elements $x_\lambda$ and $d(t)$ are the row symmetrizer and distinguished tableau permutations of [[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]], using the standard Hecke basis of [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]. The dominance poset, tableau sets and cardinality sum are [[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]], [[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]] and [[cor-sum-of-squares-of-standard-tableau-numbers]].

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Identify the objects in [F1]. Its row symmetrizer is $x_\lambda=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}T_w$, its permutation is the unique distinguished $d(t)$ carrying the row-filled tableau to $t$, and its element is $T_{d(s)}^*x_\lambda T_{d(t)}$. These are precisely [F2]'s Murphy elements. The proved integral basis in [F1] therefore gives the required $R$-basis and $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$, including the empty tableau when $n=0$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

The independent cell law says $m_{st}h\equiv\sum_v r_v m_{sv}$ modulo this ideal, with coefficients independent of $s$. Together with step 1.1 and the same finite dominance poset, these are exactly the cellular axioms and all asserted formulas. items.title: The Schur idempotent and the Schur functor for type-A q-Schur algebras
items.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$, let $q\in R^{\times}$, let $d,n\ge0$ with $d\ge n$, and let $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Write $S:=S(d,n)=\mathrm{End}_H(M)$ for the type-A q-Schur algebra with $M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)}M^{\mu}$ the direct sum of the permutation modules ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]) and let $\{\varphi_{ST}:\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n),\ S,T\in T_0(\lambda)\}$ be its cellular semistandard basis ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]] for the underlying Murphy elements and [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] for the standard basis along which this basis is defined). Put $\omega:=(1^n)\in\Lambda(d,n)$, the composition with $n$ parts equal to $1$ (legitimate because $d\ge n$), so that the Young subgroup $S_\omega$ is trivial and $m_\omega=1$; hence $$M^{\omega}=m_\omega H=H$$ is the regular right $H$-module. Let $t^{\omega}$ be the unique standard $\omega$-tableau, with entries $1,2,\dots,n$ down its single column; it is in particular the unique row-standard $\omega$-tableau whose entries increase down the column. Set $$e:=\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}\in S.$$

Then:

1. $e$ is the projection of $M$ onto the direct summand $M^{\omega}=H$ along the other summands $M^{\mu}$, $\mu\ne\omega$; in particular $e^2=e$ and $$eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})=\mathrm{End}_H(H),$$ via the algebra isomorphism $$\rho:H\longrightarrow eSe,\qquad h\longmapsto\rho_h,\qquad \rho_h(x):=hx,$$ left multiplication by $h$ on $M^{\omega}=H$ being a right $H$-module endomorphism. Here the isomorphism $eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})$ sends $efe$ to $f|_{M^{\omega}}$ and is inverted by extending an endomorphism of $M^{\omega}$ by zero on the other summands, and the identification $\mathrm{End}_H(H)\cong H$ sends an endomorphism to its value at $1$. By the construction of the semistandard basis elements $\varphi_{ST}$ (Mathas (4.13) with Corollaries 4.9 and 4.12; see the locator above), the diagonal element $\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}$ is exactly the endomorphism of $M$ that is the identity on $M^{\omega}$ and zero on all $M^{\mu}$ with $\mu\ne\omega$, which is the projection asserted above. 2. The **Schur functor** is $$F:\mathrm{mod}\text{-}S\longrightarrow\mathrm{mod}\text{-}H,\qquad F(X):=Xe=X\otimes_SSe,$$ with the right $H$-action transported along $\rho$, so that $(xe)\cdot h:=x\,\rho_h$ for $x\in X$, $h\in H$ ([[def-left-and-right-modules]]). It is exact and $R$-linear on morphisms: as a **left** $S$-module, $Se$ is the image of the left-$S$-linear projection $s\mapsto se$ on $S$, hence is a direct summand of the regular left module and is projective. Tensoring right $S$-modules with this left module is therefore exact. Equivalently, for a short exact sequence of right modules, an element $ye$ in the target lifts to $xe$ from any lift $x$ of $y$; kernels and injections are likewise preserved by the same idempotent projection. The bimodule corner action makes these maps right $H$-linear. The convention is fixed: the functor is $X\mapsto Xe$ on the right, and the left-module formula $X\mapsto eX$ is not used on this page.

Use the right-cell action identity $xC^{\lambda}_{uv}=\langle x,c^{\lambda}_uangle_\lambda c^{\lambda}_v$, obtained directly by comparing the cellular product modulo $A^{hd\lambda}$. The form radical is a submodule by [[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]. If $x$ lies outside it, choose $y=\sum_u a_uc^{\lambda}_u$ with $\langle x,yangle_\lambda=1$ and put $b_v=\sum_u a_uC^{\lambda}_{uv}$. Then $xb_v=c^{\lambda}_v$ for every $v$. Thus every vector outside the form radical generates the entire cell module; every proper submodule lies in that radical. When the form is not identically zero, the radical is therefore the unique maximal proper submodule, the quotient is simple, and the radical equals the module Jacobson radical. The same rank-one computation after any field extension, together with base change of the kernel of a finite Gram matrix, proves absolute simplicity. A form is not identically zero exactly when its radical is proper, exactly when this quotient is nonzero; nondegeneracy of the original form instead means its radical is zero.

items.statement:

([[thm-murphy-tableau-elements-form-a-cellular-basis]],

$t^\lambda$ of shape $\lambda\vdash n$
([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]), the **Murphy cell
module** $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is the right cell module $C^{\lambda}$ of the
Murphy basis: it is the free $R$-module with basis
$\{m_t:=m_{t^\lambda t}:t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$ - the classes of the
Murphy elements whose *first* index is the canonical tableau - and $H$ acts by
$m_th=\sum_vr_vm_v$ whenever
$m_{t^\lambda t}h\equiv\sum_vr_vm_{t^\lambda v}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}}$. (The
cellular action rule transforms the second index and fixes the first, so the
diagonal elements $m_{tt}$ alone do not span a submodule; the module basis is
the fixed-first-index family above.) Its **cell form** is the unique bilinear
form $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda:S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\times
S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\to R$ with

items.title: The Jantzen filtration of a lifted cell module
items.statement: Let $R$ be a principal ideal domain ([[def-principal-ideal-domain]]) with a chosen prime element $\pi$, let $F:=R/\pi R$ be the residue field, and let $M$ be a free $R$-module of finite rank ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]]) equipped with a symmetric $R$-bilinear form $\langle\ ,\ \rangle:M\times M\to R$ whose extension to the fraction field $K=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ is non-degenerate (equivalently $\det G\ne0$ for a Gram matrix $G$ of the form). For $i\ge1$ put $$M(i):=\{x\in M:\langle x,y\rangle\in\pi^iR\ \text{for all }y\in M\},\qquad M_F(i):=(M(i)+\pi M)/\pi M\subseteq M_F:=M\otimes_RF.$$ Then $M(0)=M$, the $M(i)$ are $R$-submodules with $M(i+1)\subseteq M(i)$, the descending chain $$M_F=M_F(0)\supseteq M_F(1)\supseteq M_F(2)\supseteq\cdots$$ stabilises at $0$ (that is, $M_F(z)=0$ for all sufficiently large $z$, because $\det G\ne0$), and $M_F(1)=\mathrm{rad}\,M_F$, the radical of the reduced form. This finite descending filtration is the **Jantzen filtration** of $M$ with respect to $(R,\pi,\langle\ ,\ \rangle)$. The hypotheses are exactly: $R$ a PID, $\pi$ a prime element, the form non-degenerate over $\operatorname{Frac}(R)$; no valuation-ring or DVR hypothesis is substituted, and the prime element $\pi$, its ideal $\pi R$ and the fraction field $K$ are kept distinct.
items.strategy: A definition item. Reduction gives a descending chain of finite-dimensional $F$-spaces, so it stabilises; $\det G\ne0$ makes the stable value $0$ because a vector whose pairing with every basis vector lies in all $\pi^iR$ is zero over $K$. Finally $x\in M(1)$ reduces into the radical of the reduced form by definition. This is Mathas, Chapter 5 section 2 (setup preceding Lemma 5.29), printed pp. 54-55; no choice is used.

items.title: The Hecke Jucys-Murphy action is dominance triangular
items.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, and let
$L_1,\dots,L_n$ be the Hecke Jucys-Murphy elements
([[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]]). For every $\lambda\vdash n$,
every standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ and every $1\le k\le n$ there exist
$a_v\in R$ with
$$m_tL_k=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q\,m_t+\sum_{v\rhd t}a_v\,m_v,$$
where $(m_t)_{t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)}$ is the Murphy basis of the Murphy cell
module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$
([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) and the sum is over standard
$\lambda$-tableaux $v$ strictly dominating $t$ in the dominance order on
tableaux ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]],
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). In particular $L_k$ acts on
the Murphy cell module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ with Murphy basis $(m_t)$ by a
triangular matrix whose diagonal entries are the q-content values.
Consequently the $L_k$ commute pairwise and every symmetric polynomial in
$L_1,\dots,L_n$ is central in $H$.
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A commutative ring $R$, a unit $q$, the type-A Hecke algebra $H$, its additive Jucys-Murphy elements $L_k$ and its Murphy cell module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ with basis $(m_t)$.

[F1] The standard basis multiplication, the quadratic and braid relations, and the integral row action are those of [[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]. In particular $T_i^2=(q-1)T_i+q$, and $x_\rho T_i=q x_\rho$ if $i,i+1$ lie in one row of $t^\rho$.

[F2] The integral Murphy basis, dominance ideals, cell multiplication and finite Garnir straightening are proved in [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]]. We write $I^{\rhd\lambda}=H^{\rhd\lambda}$ and $x_\lambda=m_\lambda$. The proof there supplies the dominance support rule: if $s'=ss_i$ is standard with $s\rhd s'$ and $\ell(d(s'))=\ell(d(s))+1$, multiplying any same-shape term strictly above $s$ by $T_i$ and then straightening produces only standard terms strictly above $s'$. Straightening a nonstandard row-standard tableau only raises its tableau order in the same shape. All these identities hold over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ and specialize along $v\mapsto q$.

[F3] A finite-dimensional algebra has nilpotent Jacobson radical and semisimple quotient ([[thm-jacobson-radical-is-nilpotent-and-the-quotient-is-semisimple]]). A semisimple algebra is a finite product of matrix algebras over division rings ([[thm-wedderburn-artin-theorem]]); its two-sided ideals and their quotients consequently have no nonzero nilpotent two-sided ideals.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 **Braid identities.** Put $T_i=T_{(i,i+1)}$. The reduced word for $(j,k+1)$ gives $L_{k+1}=q^{-1}(T_kL_kT_k+T_k)$. We prove $T_iL_k=L_kT_i$ whenever $i\ne k-1,k$. For $i\ge k+1$, each generator in the displayed words defining $L_k$ commutes with $T_i$. For $i\le k-3$ the recurrence and induction apply. For the remaining case $k=i+2$, put $a=T_i$, $b=T_{i+1}$ and $C=L_i$; then $bC=Cb$ by the already established disjoint case and $L_{i+2}=q^{-1}b+q^{-2}bab+q^{-2}baCab$. The braid and quadratic relations give $[a,bab]=-q[a,b]$ and $a(baCab)=(baCab)a$ (replace $aba$ by $bab$ and move $C$ past $b$), so its commutator with $a$ vanishes. Thus $L_k$ centralizes $H(S_{k-1})$; since $L_j\in H(S_{k-1})$ for $j<k$, all $L_j$ commute. Multiplying the recurrence by $T_i$ and using $T_i^2=(q-1)T_i+q$ gives $T_iL_{i+1}=L_iT_i+1+(q-1)L_{i+1}$; starring gives $T_iL_i=L_{i+1}T_i-1-(q-1)L_{i+1}$. Hence $T_i$ commutes with $L_i+L_{i+1}$ and $L_iL_{i+1}$: for the product substitute the first identity into $(L_{i+1}T_i-1-(q-1)L_{i+1})L_{i+1}$. Every symmetric polynomial is a polynomial in the elementary symmetric polynomials, and each elementary symmetric polynomial splits, at the adjacent pair, as $e_d(\widehat L_i,\widehat L_{i+1})+(L_i+L_{i+1})e_{d-1}(\widehat L_i,\widehat L_{i+1})+L_iL_{i+1}e_{d-2}(\widehat L_i,\widehat L_{i+1})$. It therefore commutes with every $T_i$ and is central. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 **Lifting smaller-rank congruences.** Here is the precise ideal check used in the induction below. Let $\tau$ be either a whole-row prefix $(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_r)$ of size $m<n$, or the prefix $(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_r,1)$ ending at the first box of the last row, of size $m<n$. In both cases $x_\lambda=h x_\tau=x_\tau h$, where $h$ is the row symmetrizer of the remaining blocks, embedded in $H_n$; in the second case its last block starts at the singleton label $m$, and no generator of $x_\tau$ meets that block. If $x_\tau L_k-cx_\tau\in I^{\rhd\tau}$ in $H_m$, expand this difference in its smaller Murphy basis. Every shape $\eta\rhd\tau$ lies in $H_mx_\eta H_m$. Embedded in $H_n$, $x_\eta$ is $x_{\kappa_\eta}$ for the partition $\kappa_\eta=(\eta,1^{n-m})$, so [F2] puts its two-sided ideal in $I^{\unrhd\kappa_\eta}$. Some prefix $j$ before the final row of $\tau$ has $\sum_{a\le j}\eta_a>\sum_{a\le j}\tau_a=\sum_{a\le j}\lambda_a$: strict dominance cannot first differ at or after the final row, where $\tau$ has total $m$. In the whole-row case the same argument permits $j<r$. Hence $\lambda$ does not dominate $\kappa_\eta$, and none of these ideals has a shape-$\lambda$ component. Multiplying the smaller congruence on the appropriate side by $h$ gives $x_\lambda L_k-cx_\lambda\in\sum_\eta I^{\unrhd\kappa_\eta}$. This difference also belongs to $I^{\unrhd\lambda}$ because both terms are in $x_\lambda H_n$. Their intersection, read in the Murphy basis, has only shapes strictly dominating $\lambda$, and the lifted congruence therefore holds modulo $I^{\rhd\lambda}$. [F2, algebra]

2.1 **An integral scalar for the central sum.** For this step work over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$, with fraction field $K=\mathbb Q(v)$. The matrix of the regular trace pairing $B(a,b)=\operatorname{Tr}_K(\ell_{ab})$ in the standard basis has entries in $A$. At $v=1$ it is the matrix $n!\,\delta_{u,w^{-1}}$, since a nonidentity permutation has no fixed point in the regular permutation action. Its determinant is nonzero, so $B$ is nondegenerate over $K$. If $a$ belongs to the Jacobson radical $J$ then $ab\in J$ is nilpotent for every $b$, by [F3]; thus $\ell_{ab}$ is nilpotent and has trace zero. Nondegeneracy forces $J=0$, so $H_K$ is semisimple. In its cell layer $I^{\unrhd\lambda}_K/I^{\rhd\lambda}_K$, [F2] identifies multiplication with $X\cdot Y=XG_\lambda Y$ on $d\times d$ matrices, $d=|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|$. If $G_\lambda$ were singular, the nonzero subspace $N=\{X:G_\lambda X=0\}$ would be a two-sided ideal of this layer with $N^2=0$, contradicting [F3]. Hence $G_\lambda$ is invertible and $X\mapsto G_\lambda X$ identifies the layer with $\operatorname{Mat}_d(K)$. A central element of $H_K$ acts on this layer by a bimodule endomorphism of that matrix algebra, necessarily a scalar: its value at the identity commutes with every matrix and therefore is a scalar matrix. Applied to $Z_n=\sum_kL_k$, central by step 1.1, this shows that its matrix on the cell module is $\alpha_\lambda I_d$ over $K$. The cell action matrix already has entries in $A$, so $\alpha_\lambda\in A$, and freeness over $A$ makes the identity hold integrally and after every base change to $R$. Thus $m_tZ_n=\alpha_\lambda m_t$ for every $t$, without any assumption on the specialized cell form or its head. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 **Transport along standard adjacent swaps.** Suppose $s'=ss_i$ is standard with $s\rhd s'$ and length increasing by one, and suppose $m_sL_k=r_s(k)m_s+\sum_{u\rhd s}a_um_u$ for all $k$. By [F1], $m_{s'}=m_sT_i$. For $k\ne i,i+1$ step 1.1 gives $m_{s'}L_k=m_sL_kT_i$, and [F2] puts every error strictly above $s'$. For $k=i+1$, the same step gives $m_{s'}L_{i+1}=m_s(L_iT_i+1+(q-1)L_{i+1})$; its coefficient at $m_{s'}$ is $r_s(i)$, since all remaining terms are strictly above $s'$. The second adjacent identity similarly gives coefficient $r_s(i+1)$ at $m_{s'}$ for $L_i$. Thus the diagonal data are transposed in positions $i,i+1$ and unchanged elsewhere. Every standard tableau is reachable from $t^\lambda$ by such standard length-increasing swaps: reverse a right-descent reduction of $d(t)$; the two consecutive entries at a descent lie in incomparable cells, so their interchange remains standard. Consequently diagonal data at the row-filled tableau determine the asserted diagonals at every standard tableau. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 **Row-filled induction away from the final singleton.** Induct on $n$, the cases $n=0,1$ being immediate, and on $k$ within the row-filled tableau. If $k$ is in a row which is not the last row, choose the whole-row prefix $\tau$ ending with that row. It has size $m<n$, its row-filled tableau has no more dominant standard tableaux, and the induction on rank gives $x_\tau L_k=[\operatorname{content}_{t^\tau}(k)]_q x_\tau$ modulo $I^{\rhd\tau}$. Lift by step 1.2. If $k$ is in the last row but not its first column, $T_{k-1}$ belongs to its row subgroup, and the recurrence gives $m_{t^\lambda}L_k=(1+q[\operatorname{content}_{t^\lambda}(k-1)]_q)m_{t^\lambda}=[\operatorname{content}_{t^\lambda}(k)]_q m_{t^\lambda}$, by induction on $k$ and $[c+1]_q=1+q[c]_q$. If $k<n$ is in the first column of the last row, use the singleton-ended prefix $\tau$ of step 1.2 and induction on its smaller rank. These arguments leave only $k=n$ for a shape $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_r,1)$. All $L_k$ with $k<n$ have already been shown to act on $m_{t^\lambda}$ by their claimed scalars. Step 2.1 then supplies $m_{t^\lambda}L_n=r_nm_{t^\lambda}$ for some $r_n\in R$. Step 2.2 consequently applies with these diagonal data to every standard tableau; at this point all $L_k$ are triangular, though $r_n$ remains to be identified. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 1.2, induction, algebra]

4.1 **The final singleton is fixed by one Garnir calculation.** In the remaining shape let $i$ be the first entry in row $r$ of $t^\lambda$ and put $t=t^\lambda s_{n-1}\cdots s_{i+1}$. Then $t$ is standard, its last row contains $i+1$, and its penultimate row contains $i,i+2,\dots,n$. Step 2.2 gives $m_tL_i=[1-r]_q m_t+\sum_{v\rhd t}a_vm_v$ and $m_tL_{i+1}=r_nm_t+\sum_{v\rhd t}b_vm_v$. The tableau $g:=ts_i$ is exactly the Garnir tableau for the first-column belt $i,\dots,n$ between the last two rows. For $j=i,\dots,n$, let $u_j$ have last-row entry $j$ and the other belt labels increasingly in row $r$. The finite belt identity of [F2] gives $\sum_{j=i}^n x_\lambda T_{d(u_j)}\equiv0\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}}$: its other side is a sum of multiples of the symmetrizer obtained by merging these two rows, whose sorted shape strictly dominates $\lambda$. Here $u_i=g$, $u_{i+1}=t$, and all $u_j$ with $j>i+1$ are standard and strictly dominate $t$. The length-increasing row rule gives $m_tT_i=x_\lambda T_{d(g)}+I^{\rhd\lambda}$, so the belt identity explicitly yields $m_tT_i=-m_t-\sum_{j>i+1}m_{u_j}$. Put $U=\operatorname{span}\{m_v:v\rhd t\}$. Step 3.1 and transport show $UL_i\subseteq U$. Also $UT_i\subseteq U$: dominance forces each $v\unrhd t$ to agree with $t$ on the filled first $r-1$ rows and to place $i$ in node $(r,1)$. If $i+1$ occupies the singleton last row, all remaining labels must occupy row $r$ increasingly, forcing $v=t$. Thus every $v\rhd t$ places $i+1$ in $(r,2)$, and the row rule gives $m_vT_i=q m_v$. (If $\lambda_r=1$, the higher span is zero.) Working modulo $U$, the recurrence now gives $m_tL_{i+1}=q^{-1}m_t(T_iL_iT_i+T_i)=q^{-1}([1-r]_q-1)m_t=[-r]_q m_t$. Comparing its coefficient at $m_t$ proves $r_n=[-r]_q$, exactly the content of the final singleton. This completes the rank induction and identifies all row-filled diagonals. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 **The required flag and the initial left generator.** Step 2.2 now gives $m_tL_k=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q m_t+\sum_{v\rhd t}a_vm_v$ for every standard $t$, over the given ring. Order the standard tableaux by any linear extension with the most dominant first. The spans of initial segments are stable under all $L_k$, and their successive rank-one quotients have exactly the q-content diagonals; this proves the claimed common triangular flag. Commutativity and symmetric-polynomial centrality were established independently in step 1.1. In particular the maximal tableau $t^\lambda$ has the exact eigenrelation $m_{t^\lambda}L_k=[\operatorname{content}_{t^\lambda}(k)]_q m_{t^\lambda}$. Since $L_k^*=L_k$, starring its defining cell congruence gives the corresponding left-cell generator relation $L_k z_\lambda=[\operatorname{content}_{t^\lambda}(k)]_q z_\lambda$. For the multiplicative normalization $X_k=1+(q-1)L_k$ this reads $X_k z_\lambda=q^{\operatorname{content}_{t^\lambda}(k)}z_\lambda$, using $1+(q-1)[c]_q=q^c$ for all integral $c$. These identities concern the cell generator, hence hold after taking the indicated cell quotient; they do not assert the same equality for the raw symmetrizer in $H$. All formulas specialize from $A$ to $R$, and no quantum integer or factorial is inverted in the specialized algebra. [step 1.1, step 2.2, step 4.1, F2, algebra] ∎

items.title: The simple type-A Hecke modules are indexed by e-regular partitions
items.statement:
Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, let
$e=e(F,q)\in\{2,3,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ be the quantum characteristic
([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]) and let
$H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for $n\ge0$. For $\lambda\vdash n$ let $S^{\lambda}$ be the
Hecke Specht module and $D^{\lambda}=S^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}$ its
cell-form quotient ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]). Then:

1. $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if $\lambda$ is $e$-regular
   ([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]);
2. $\{D^{\lambda}:\lambda\vdash n\text{ is }e\text{-regular}\}$ is a complete
   set of pairwise non-isomorphic absolutely irreducible $H$-modules;
3. $H$ is split semisimple if and only if $e>n$ (including $e=\infty$); when
   $e\le n$ the algebra has nonzero radical.

This is the exact root-of-unity replacement for the ordinary Specht
classification. At $q=1$ in characteristic $p>0$ it specialises to the
classification of the simple $F[S_n]$-modules by $p$-regular partitions
([[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]). No
semisimplicity is assumed and no choice principle is used.
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$, a unit $q$, the type-A Hecke algebra $H$, its Murphy cells $C_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$ and form quotients $D_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$, and the ordinary signed-conjugate normalization in the Statement.

[F1] The nonzero cell-form quotients are pairwise distinct absolutely simple modules and exhaust the simples. A quotient is nonzero precisely when its form is not identically zero; a zero form quotient makes no assertion about the actual module head ([[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]]).

[F2] The actual ordinary module/form bridge gives $S^\lambda=C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ and $D^\lambda=D_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$, with $\theta(T_i)=(q-1)-T_i$ an involution commuting with star. Pullback is exact and preserves nonzero modules and simplicity ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]). Conjugation exchanges regular and restricted partitions ([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]).

[F3] The locally proved Jucys–Murphy elements commute and preserve a common tableau flag of each Murphy cell, with diagonal word $([c_t(1)]_q,\ldots,[c_t(n)]_q)$, where $c_t(a)$ is the integer node content. The row-filled maximal tableau has an exact eigenrelation ([[thm-hecke-jucys-murphy-action-is-dominance-triangular]]).

[F4] Cellular support gives $[C_{\mathrm M}(\eta):D_{\mathrm M}(\rho)]=0$ unless $\eta\unrhd\rho$, and gives diagonal multiplicity one when that quotient is nonzero ([[cor-cellular-decomposition-matrices-are-dominance-unitriangular]]).

[F5] The integral Murphy basis, dominance ideals, row action and finite Garnir straightening are valid over $A=\mathbb Z[Q,Q^{-1}]$ and commute with every base change ([[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]], [[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]). For a row group $S_\alpha$, $x_\alpha^2=[\alpha]!_Qx_\alpha$ by length-additive parabolic cosets; $[\alpha]!_Q=\prod_j[\alpha_j]!_Q$ ([[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]]).

[F6] At $q=1$, the quantum characteristic is the field characteristic when positive, and is infinity in characteristic zero ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]); the ordinary group labels are the regular Specht-head labels ([[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]). The Jacobson radical of a finite-dimensional algebra is the intersection of the annihilators of its simple modules ([[def-jacobson-radical-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Use finite joint-primary projections without presupposing which labels survive. The regular right module has a cellular filtration with quotients copies of the cells; refining their common flags in [F3] gives a simultaneous triangular flag on it. Thus each $L_a$ is annihilated by a polynomial $\prod_b(X-b)^N$, with finitely many diagonal values $b\in F$ and $N\ge\dim H$. Polynomial Bezout and the Chinese remainder construction give $p_{a,b}$ congruent to one modulo $(X-b)^N$ and zero modulo the other factors. Substituting $L_a$ gives commuting idempotents. For a joint word $\xi$, their product $P_\xi$ is idempotent in $H$ and on a cell flag has diagonal one exactly at tableaux with word $\xi$, zero elsewhere. An idempotent has zero image if and only if all these diagonal entries vanish: its triangular matrix would otherwise be nilpotent and idempotent, hence zero. The vector-space functor $M\mapsto MP_\xi$ is exact on $H$-modules, because a lift $x$ of $y=yP_\xi$ can be replaced by $xP_\xi$, and kernels are preserved. No centrality or $H$-submodule assertion for this image is needed. [F3, F5, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 For finite $e$, equality of two diagonal values $[a]_q,[b]_q$ is equivalent to $a\equiv b\pmod e$. Indeed $[a]_q-[b]_q=q^b[a-b]_q$ for all integers, including negative integers. When $q\ne1$, $e$ is the multiplicative order of $q$, and when $q=1$, $e=\operatorname{char}F$ and the q-integer is the integer reduced to $F$. Thus a joint word is exactly a residue word in the node convention $c-r\pmod e$. [given, F3, F6, algebra]

1.3 Prove the complete ladder-boundary comparison. Put $L(s,c)=(e-1)s+c-e$. Suppose $\alpha$ is restricted, every occupied node has $L<l$, and the addable ladder-$l$ set is nonempty. Set $C=l+e-1$, $T=\lfloor C/(e-1)\rfloor$, $d=C-(e-1)T\in\{0,\ldots,e-2\}$ and $u_s=C-(e-1)s$. For $1\le s\le T$, $0\le\alpha_s\le u_s$, and no positive row occurs beyond $T$. The deficits $h_s=u_s-\alpha_s$ are nonnegative and satisfy $h_{s+1}-h_s=\alpha_s-\alpha_{s+1}-(e-1)\le0$. An addable ladder-$l$ row has deficit zero; thereafter every deficit is zero. Consecutive such rows have width difference $e-1>0$, so the ladder addables form a terminal interval $s_0,\ldots,T$. A first equality row that is not addable simply precedes this interval. Adding its bottommost $k$ nodes therefore adds in rows $T-k+1,\ldots,T$. The length of $\alpha$ is $T$ for $d>0$ and $T-1$ for $d=0$, including the empty case $T=1,d=0$. If $\beta\unrhd\alpha$ has the same size, its length is at most that of $\alpha$, by the prefix inequality at that length. For $d=0$ all addable rows of $\beta$ are at most $T$. For $d>0$ the sole possible extra row is $T+1$, with residue $-T$, different from $i=l\bmod e=d+1-T\bmod e$ since $1\le d+1<e$. Hence every addable $i$-node of $\beta$ lies in a row at most $T$. If $\gamma$ adds any $k$ of these initial addables, at row cutoff $r$ its prefix increment is at least $\max(0,k-\max(T-r,0))$, exactly the increment for the bottommost-$k$ extension $\delta$ of $\alpha$. Adding $\beta$'s prefix inequalities proves $\gamma\unrhd\delta$. This holds for every $k$ simultaneously and needs no same-content premise. [given, construct, algebra]

1.4 Prove the converse on actual Gram entries. Work in the universal Laurent domain $A$ and write $x_\eta=x_{B_1}\cdots x_{B_k}$ for the symmetrizers of the consecutive row-label intervals. For a row-standard tableau $t$, multiply $x_\eta T_{d(t)}$ successively by these symmetrizers and straighten modulo $I^{\rhd\eta}$. The row calculation is as follows. Once rows before $j$ agree with $t^\eta$, let $\beta_s$ count the labels of $B_j$ in row $s\ge j$; $\sum\beta_s=\eta_j$. Sort these labels in row-reading order to obtain $u$, so $t=uw$ with $w\in S_{B_j}$ and additive length. Therefore multiplication by $x_{B_j}$ first contributes $Q^{\ell(w)}$. The row-parabolic intersection on these labels is $S_{\beta_j}\times\cdots\times S_{\beta_k}$. Expanding its length-additive cosets gives the further factor $[\beta]!_Q$: each common intersection permutation contributes its inversion weight. After removing this intersection, the remaining sum belongs to the two-sided row ideal for the composition $(\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_{j-1},\eta_j,\eta_j-\beta_j,\ldots,\eta_k-\beta_k)$, with zero parts omitted. This is the finite row-double-coset calculation in [F5], using no factorial inversion. If its sorted partition does not lie below $\eta$, its intersection with $I^{\unrhd\eta}$ has only strictly higher shapes and this term vanishes in the cell. Otherwise its prefix inequality at $j+1$ gives $\beta_j\ge\eta_j-\eta_{j+1}$ (the first $j-1$ parts are unchanged, and sorting can only increase the indicated prefix). Straightening retains the now fixed first $j$ canonical rows: maximal prefix counts on those rows cannot be raised further. This proves the same row calculation inductively for every $j$. All coefficients remain in $A$. [F5, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 For restricted $\eta$, number its nodes by increasing $L$, taking lower rows first on a tie, to obtain $t_\eta$. Moving right increases $L$ by one and moving down by $e-1$, so it is standard. The diagrams $\alpha_l$ of nodes with $L<l$ and $\delta_l$ with $L\le l$ are restricted: their row widths are the minimum of the restricted widths of $\eta$ and the positive part of the affine cutoff bound, each having adjacent difference at most $e-1$. A node on ladder $l$ forces every lower positive position on that ladder to be occupied, since $\eta_{s+1}\ge\eta_s-(e-1)$. Thus $\delta_l$ adds the bottommost $a_l$ ladder addables to $\alpha_l$. Any competing standard tableau with the same full residue word has, in the corresponding block, $a_l$ additions all of residue $l$. Every such node was addable before the block: adding an $i$-node creates new addable corners only of residues $i+1,i-1$, distinct from $i$ for $e\ge2$. Starting with the empty diagrams, step 1.3 inductively shows its shape dominates $\delta_l$ at every completed block, and hence its final shape dominates $\eta$. No strictly lower shape has the word of $t_\eta$, and no same-shape tableau uniqueness is asserted. [step 1.3, construct, algebra]

3.1 Choose $P_\xi$ for the word of $t_\eta$. It has nonzero image on $C_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$ and zero image on every $C_{\mathrm M}(\rho)$ with $\rho\lhd\eta$, by steps 1.2 and 2.1. Therefore it has zero image on their form quotients. Apply the exact projection to a composition series of $C_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$. Some constituent has nonzero image; by [F1] and [F4] it is a nonzero $D_{\mathrm M}(\rho)$ with $\rho\unlhd\eta$. The exclusion forces $\rho=\eta$, proving the restricted Murphy quotient nonzero over the original field. This is a joint-word and cellular-support proof, not an import of cellular/crystal label identification. [F1, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 If $\eta_j-\eta_{j+1}\ge e$ for some $j$, every surviving term at that row has $\beta_j\ge e$ by step 1.4 and is divisible by $[e]!_Q$. Later multiplication and straightening cannot remove this polynomial factor. Every Gram entry is the coefficient of $x_\eta$ in $x_\eta T_{d(s)}T_{d(t)}^*x_\eta$ modulo higher shapes; first expand its middle factor in the row-module basis and apply the proved row calculation. Thus every entry is divisible by $[e]!_Q$. Specializing $Q$ to $q$ makes that factor zero, so the entire Murphy form vanishes and $D_{\mathrm M}(\eta)=0$. This concerns a common divisor of entries, not a product-of-hooks formula for a determinant. Combining with step 3.1 proves the finite-$e$ Murphy criterion. [F1, F5, step 1.4, step 3.1, algebra]

4.2 For $e>n$, including infinity, distinct standard tableaux of any shapes have distinct full diagonal words. At their first unequal step the preceding diagram has size $a-1$; its distinct addable-corner contents differ by a nonzero integer of absolute value at most $a\le n$, so their q-integers differ. Induction recovers every next node. Consequently every tableau word of $C_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$ occurs in no strictly lower cell. Exact projections as in step 3.1 and diagonal multiplicity one in [F4] show that all $\dim C_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$ flag factors occur in $D_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$; thus this quotient has the full cell dimension and its form radical is zero. In particular at $e=\infty$ every partition is restricted and has nonzero quotient. At $n=0$ the unique cell is $F$ with norm one. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Establish the complete semisimplicity clause. Put $f_\eta=\dim C_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$ and $d_\eta=\dim D_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$, with zero for a zero quotient. The Murphy basis gives $\dim H=\sum_\eta f_\eta^2$. On each nonzero quotient its nondegenerate form and the cell law supply all rank-one operators. Since the cells are right modules, their action gives a surjective algebra map $H\to\operatorname{End}_F(D_{\mathrm M}(\eta))^{\mathrm{op}}$, a full matrix algebra after transpose. Its kernels are distinct maximal two-sided ideals: equality would give the same matrix-algebra simple module, contradicting [F1]. They are pairwise comaximal. Their finite product map is surjective: for each kernel $I_a$ and each other $I_b$ choose $u_{ab}\in I_b$ congruent to one modulo $I_a$, multiply over $b\ne a$, and use these elements to isolate each prescribed matrix component. Its kernel is the radical by the complete simple list and [F6]. Hence $\dim(H/\operatorname{rad}H)=\sum_\eta d_\eta^2$. Step 4.2 makes this equal to $\dim H$ when $e>n$, giving an isomorphism with a product of full matrix algebras over $F$. When finite $e\le n$, the one-dimensional Murphy row cell has norm $[n]!_q=0$, since $x_{(n)}^2=[n]!_q x_{(n)}$. Its quotient dimension is zero while its cell dimension is one; every other $d_\eta\le f_\eta$. The dimension sum is therefore strictly smaller and $\operatorname{rad}H\ne0$. This proves both directions of part 3 without any claim that some Specht module must be reducible. [F1, F5, F6, step 4.2, algebra]

6.1 Apply the same exact involution to every Murphy quotient: $D^\lambda=D_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ is nonzero exactly when $\lambda'$ is restricted, equivalently when $\lambda$ is regular. The nonzero quotients remain pairwise distinct absolutely simple and complete by [F1] and [F2]. This proves parts 1 and 2, and step 5.1 gives part 3. At $q=1$, [F6] gives precisely the ordinary $p$-regular group classification, including characteristic two; no splitting or semisimplicity assumption was made. All selections and polynomial computations were finite, so no choice principle is used. [F1, F2, F6, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 5.1] ∎

## Remarks

The finite ladder-boundary lemma, joint-primary projection argument and row-entry divisibility are local proofs. The cited manuscript documents their source; its erroneous displayed ladder slope and unsupported single-node truncation sentence are replaced by the complete simultaneous-block comparison above. The richest original classification and radical assertions are retained. Zero cell-form quotients are distinguished from actual module heads throughout.

items.title: The type-A Hecke decomposition matrix is dominance unitriangular
items.statement:
Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, $e=e(F,q)$ and $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$
([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]). For
$\lambda\vdash n$ and $e$-regular $\mu\vdash n$ let
$$d_{\lambda\mu}:=[S^{\lambda}:D^{\mu}],$$
the multiplicity of $D^{\mu}$ in a composition series of the Specht module
$S^{\lambda}$ ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]],
[[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]]). Then
$$d_{\mu\mu}=1\qquad\text{and}\qquad d_{\lambda\mu}\ne0\ \Longrightarrow\ \mu\unrhd\lambda,$$
where $\unrhd$ is the dominance order on partitions
([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]): a simple factor $D^{\mu}$ of
$S^{\lambda}$ can occur only if the $e$-regular label $\mu$ dominates
$\lambda$. Equivalently the decomposition matrix $(d_{\lambda\mu})$ is
unitriangular along dominance. This constrains but does not compute the
entries: no off-diagonal decomposition number is determined by cellularity.
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$, $q\in F^{\times}$, $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ with Specht modules $S^{\lambda}$ and simple quotients $D^{\mu}$ in the signed conjugate normalization ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]), together with the dominance order on partitions of $n$ ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]).

[F1] ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) $S^{\lambda}=(S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$ and $D^{\mu}=(D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$ for the conjugate partitions, where $S^{\nu}_{\mathrm M}$ is the Murphy cell module and $\theta$ is the involutive automorphism $\theta(T_i)=-qT_i^{-1}$; pullback along $\theta$ is exact and preserves submodules, quotients, composition multiplicities and simplicity.

[F2] ([[cor-cellular-decomposition-matrices-are-dominance-unitriangular]]) For the Murphy cellular basis of $H$ the composition multiplicity $[S^{\nu}_{\mathrm M}:D^{\rho}_{\mathrm M}]$ satisfies $[S^{\rho}_{\mathrm M}:D^{\rho}_{\mathrm M}]=1$ whenever $D^{\rho}_{\mathrm M}\ne0$ and is zero unless $\nu\unrhd\rho$.

[F3] ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]) Conjugation reverses dominance: $\lambda'\unrhd\mu'$ if and only if $\mu\unrhd\lambda$.

[F4] ([[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]]) $D^{\mu}\ne0$ exactly for the $e$-regular $\mu$.



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Invariance of composition multiplicities under the normalisation: by [F1] the twist $(-)^\theta$ is an exact equivalence of module categories with inverse $(-)^\theta$ itself, so it is additive on short exact sequences and carries composition series to composition series; hence $[S^{\lambda}:D^{\mu}]=[S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}:D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}]$ for all $\lambda\vdash n$ and $e$-regular $\mu\vdash n$. [given, F1, F4]

2.1 Vanishing: if $d_{\lambda\mu}\ne0$, then $[S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}:D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}]\ne0$ by step 1.1, so $\lambda'\unrhd\mu'$ by [F2], and conjugation reversal [F3] gives $\mu\unrhd\lambda$. [step 1.1, F2, F3]

2.2 Diagonal: taking $\lambda=\mu$ in step 1.1 gives $d_{\mu\mu}=[S^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}:D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}]=1$ by [F2]. [step 1.1, F2]

3.1 Assembly: steps 2.1 and 2.2 are exactly the two claims; ordering the rows and columns of $(d_{\lambda\mu})$ by any linear extension of dominance displays the unitriangular shape, and no off-diagonal entry is determined by the cellular structure. At $q=1$ the statement specialises to the classical symmetric-group unitriangularity of [[thm-symmetric-group-decomposition-matrix-is-dominance-unitriangular]] by [F4]. [step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎

items.title: Jantzen layer dimensions sum to the Gram determinant valuation
items.statement:
In the setting of [[def-jantzen-filtration-of-a-lifted-cell-module]] ($R$ a PID, $\pi$ a prime element, $F=R/\pi R$, $M$ free of finite rank with a form whose extension to $K=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ is non-degenerate), let $
u_\pi$ be the $\pi$-adic valuation normalised by $
u_\pi(\pi)=1$ and let $G\in R\setminus\{0\}$ be the Gram determinant of the form with respect to any $R$-basis of $M$. Then $$
u_\pi(G)=\sum_{i>0}\dim_FM_F(i),$$ where $M_F(i)$ are the Jantzen layers of [[def-jantzen-filtration-of-a-lifted-cell-module]]; in particular the sum is finite and independent of the chosen basis.
items.strategy:
Use the Smith normal form ([[thm-smith-normal-form-existence-over-a-pid]]) to choose bases $e_1,\dots,e_d$ of $M$ and $f_1,\dots,f_d$ of $\mathrm{Hom}_R(M,R)$ with $\langle e_i,f_jangle=\delta_{ij}r_i$, $r_i\in R\setminus\{0\}$; non-degeneracy over $K$ is exactly what produces the nonzero $r_i$. Then $G=\pm\prod_ir_i$, so $
u_\pi(G)=\sum_i
u_\pi(r_i)$. On the other hand $x=\sum_ia_ie_i$ lies in $M(k)$ if and only if $
u_\pi(a_ir_i)\ge k$ for all $i$, so $M_F(k)$ has as basis the images of those $e_i$ with $
u_\pi(r_i)\ge k$; hence $\dim_FM_F(k)=\#\{i:
u_\pi(r_i)\ge k\}$ and $\sum_{k>0}\dim_FM_F(k)=\sum_i
u_\pi(r_i)$. This is Mathas, Lemma 5.29 (Jantzen), printed p. 58; no choice is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The field, parameter, stable range and modules in the Statement; all modules are right modules and multiplication in $S=\operatorname{End}_H(M)$ is ordinary composition $(fg)(x)=f(g(x))$.

[F1] The actual projection $e$ onto $M^\omega=H$, for $\omega=(1^n,0^{d-n})$, satisfies $e^2=e$ and $eSe\cong H$ by left multiplication $\rho(h)(a)=ha$. The functor is $X\mapsto Xe$ ([[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]]).

[F2] The legitimate semistandard cellular construction is supported from $M^{\operatorname{type}(T)}$ to $M^{\operatorname{type}(S)}$ and sends its generating $m_{\operatorname{type}(T)}h$ to $m_{ST}h$; its star swaps $S,T$ and its right-cell coefficients fix the first index modulo higher shapes. The Weyl cell basis is $(w_T)_T$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Only the actual summand projections are weight idempotents; no assertion that all diagonal cellular elements are idempotent is used.

[F3] The independent Murphy cellular datum uses $m_{st}=T_{d(s)}^*x_\lambda T_{d(t)}$, with its higher ideal $I^{\rhd\lambda}$, right cell basis $(c_t)_t$ and form $G_\lambda$ characterized by $m_{as}m_{tb}\equiv G_\lambda(c_s,c_t)m_{ab}$ modulo that ideal ([[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]]).

[F4] The nonzero cell-form quotients are pairwise distinct absolutely irreducible modules; when the form is not identically zero its radical is the unique maximal submodule. These are the general cellular conclusions of [[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]].

[F5] The genuine ordinary bridge gives $P(\alpha)\cong C_{\mathrm M}(\alpha')^\theta$ and an explicit unit-scaled form identity, hence $D_{\mathrm{DJ}}(\alpha)\cong D_{\mathrm M}(\alpha')^\theta$ including zero quotients. This is the page's signed Specht normalization, and $\theta$ is an involutive algebra automorphism whose pullback is exact ([[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]], [[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]).

[F6] The full type-A classifier proves that $D_{\mathrm M}(\nu)$ is nonzero precisely for $e_q$-restricted $\nu$ over the original field, including the finite-$e_q$ range and the empty partition; its ordinary-label statement is transported through the signed-conjugate form bridge, not inferred from a group-only specialization ([[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]], [[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Under [F1], $\rho(h)\rho(k)=\rho(hk)$ because both act on $H$ by left multiplication, so the identification uses $H$, without an opposite algebra. The functor $X\mapsto Xe$ is exact: for a short exact sequence, a lift $x$ of an element $y\in X''e$ yields the lift $xe$, and an element in the kernel lies in $X'$ and is fixed by $e$, hence lies in $X'e$. The tensor description uses the $(S,eSe)$-bimodule $Se$, which is a direct summand as a left $S$-module. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The support in [F2] gives $e\varphi_{ST}e=\delta_{\operatorname{type}(S),\omega}\delta_{\operatorname{type}(T),\omega}\varphi_{ST}$ and $w_Te=\delta_{\operatorname{type}(T),\omega}w_T$. Semistandard tableaux of type $\omega$ have each label once and are exactly standard tableaux. For standard $s,t$, their defining sum $m_{st}$ has one term, so $\varphi_{st}|_H(a)=m_{st}a$ and $\rho^{-1}(\varphi_{st})=m_{st}$. Thus the higher Schur ideal cuts out exactly $I^{\rhd\lambda}$ in the corner. Read the Schur right-cell law with first index any standard tableau of type $\omega$; coefficient independence permits this choice. Restricting the multiplication by $\rho(h)$ to $H$ gives $m_{st}h$, so its coefficients are the Murphy right-cell coefficients. Consequently $\Psi_\lambda:W^\lambda e\to C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$, $w_t\mapsto c_t$, is an $H$-isomorphism. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 By the Schur cell product, $\varphi_{as}\varphi_{tb}\equiv B_\lambda(w_s,w_t)\varphi_{ab}$ modulo higher Schur shapes, with coefficient independent of the outer indices. Choose all four indices standard of shape $\lambda$ and type $\omega$. They lie in $eSe$; applying $\rho^{-1}$, or evaluating their endomorphisms at $1\in H$, gives $m_{as}m_{tb}\equiv B_\lambda(w_s,w_t)m_{ab}$ modulo $I^{\rhd\lambda}$. The unique coefficient in [F3] is $G_\lambda(c_s,c_t)$, proving $B_\lambda|_{W^\lambda e}=\Psi_\lambda^*G_\lambda$ exactly, with factor $1$. [F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Since $e^*=e$, contravariance gives $B_\lambda(xe,y(1-e))=B_\lambda(x,y(1-e)e)=0$. The decomposition $W^\lambda=W^\lambda e\oplus W^\lambda(1-e)$ is therefore orthogonal. A vector in $W^\lambda e$ pairs trivially with its complement, so it is in the restricted form radical exactly when it lies in $\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{form}}W^\lambda$. Since the latter is an $S$-submodule, $\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{form}}(W^\lambda e)=(\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{form}}W^\lambda)e$. This holds even if the corner form is identically zero. [F2, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 For the canonical semistandard tableau $T^\lambda$ of shape and type $\lambda$, the map $\varphi_{T^\lambda,T^\lambda}$ is the actual projection onto $M^\lambda$: it sends $m_\lambda h$ to itself and is zero on every other summand. Its square equals itself, so the Schur cell product gives $B_\lambda(w_{T^\lambda},w_{T^\lambda})=1$. Hence the Weyl form quotient is nonzero and is its simple head $L^\lambda$ by [F4]. Exactness, step 4.1 and step 3.1 give $L^\lambda e\cong W^\lambda e/(\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{form}}W^\lambda)e\cong C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)/\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{form}}C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)=D_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$, including when this corner quotient is zero. [F2, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 By [F6] and step 5.1, $L^\lambda e\ne0$ precisely for $e_q$-restricted $\lambda$. Apply the exact functor to a finite composition series of $W^\lambda$: every factor $L^\nu$ gives $D_{\mathrm M}(\nu)$ or zero. Delete repeated terms. The remaining factors are the distinct nonzero Murphy simples in [F4], giving $[W^\lambda:L^\nu]=[C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):D_{\mathrm M}(\nu)]$ for each $e_q$-restricted $\nu$. No multiplicity preservation is asserted for a killed simple label. [F4, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Apply [F5] and the involution $\theta$ to obtain $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')\cong(S^\lambda)^\theta$ and $D_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')\cong(D^\lambda)^\theta$. Replacing the Weyl label by $\lambda'$ in steps 2.1 and 5.1 gives the ordinary dictionary, including zero quotients. Conjugation makes $\lambda'$ restricted precisely when $\lambda$ is regular. Twisting both modules by the same exact equivalence preserves composition multiplicities, so step 6.1 gives $[W^{\lambda'}:L^{\nu'}]=[S^\lambda:D^\nu]$ for regular $\nu$. The genuine unit-scaled ordinary form bridge in [F5] also identifies these with the historical DJ polytabloid modules and quotients. At $n=0$, $e=1$ and each form has value $1$, so the same proof includes the empty partition. [F4, F5, F6, step 2.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Separated Hecke residues give seminormal idempotents and bases
items.statement:
Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, let $e=e(F,q)$ and assume $e>n$ (with $e=\infty$ allowed); let $\lambda\vdash n$, $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$, and let $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ be the Murphy cell module with Murphy basis $(m_t)_{t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)}$ ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]).

1. (**Separation**) If $s,t$ are standard $\lambda$-tableaux with $[\operatorname{content}_s(k)]_q=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q$ for all $1\le k\le n$ then $s=t$. More precisely, if the q-content values agree for all $k\notin\{i,i+1\}$ for some $i$, then $s=t$ or $t=s(i\ i+1)$. 2. (**Idempotents**) Let $\mathcal R_k$ be the set of distinct q-content values of the entry $k$ over standard tableaux of **all** partitions of $n$. For a standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ define $$F_t:=\prod_{k=1}^{n}\ \prod_{\substack{c\in\mathcal R_k\\        c\ne[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q}}        \frac{L_k-c}{[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q-c}\in F[L_1,\ldots,L_n].$$ These are orthogonal idempotents of $H$; their actions on $S_{\mathrm M}^\lambda$ project onto the corresponding simultaneous eigenlines. Put $f_t=m_tF_t$. Then $f_tL_k=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_qf_t$ and $f_t=m_t+\sum_{s\rhd t}a_sm_s$. The global content sets are essential for the asserted idempotency in $H$, rather than only the induced same-shape endomorphisms. 3. (**Orthogonal seminormal basis**) $\{f_t:t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is a basis of $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ satisfying $f_tF_s=\delta_{ts}f_t$ and $\langle f_s,f_t\rangle_\lambda=\delta_{st}\langle f_t,f_t\rangle_\lambda$; it is the **seminormal basis** of the Murphy cell module. 4. (**Generator action**) Let $s$ be a standard $\lambda$-tableau, $1\le i<n$ and $t:=s(i\ i+1)$, and put $\rho:=\operatorname{content}_s(i)-\operatorname{content}_s(i+1)\in\mathbb Z$. If $i$ and $i+1$ lie in the same row of $s$ then $f_sT_i=q\,f_s$; if they lie in the same column then $f_sT_i=-f_s$; otherwise $t$ is standard and $$f_sT_i=\alpha_i(s)\,f_t-\frac{1}{[\rho]_q}f_s,\qquad \alpha_i(s):=\begin{cases}1,&s\rhd t,\\[1mm]\dfrac{[1+\rho]_q[1-\rho]_q}{[\rho]_q[-\rho]_q},&t\rhd s,\end{cases}$$ where $[-\rho]_q$ is the extended quantum integer of [[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]] and for the swapped tableau $\operatorname{content}_t(i)-\operatorname{content}_t(i+1)=-\rho$. No semisimplicity of $H$ is assumed and no choice principle is used.
